reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India NTEP
clinicalPearls: The most common form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis, especially in India, most often involving the cervical lymph nodes (historically termed scrofula)
Typically presents as a firm, painless, gradually enlarging node or matted nodes, sometimes progressing to a fluctuant cold abscess or discharging sinus
Constitutional symptoms such as fever, night sweats and weight loss may be absent, so a chronic painless node warrants consideration of tuberculosis in endemic settings
Fine-needle aspiration cytology showing granulomas with caseation is a key first-line, minimally invasive diagnostic step
Molecular testing such as cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification on aspirate improves sensitivity and detects rifampicin resistance
Paradoxical enlargement of nodes during or after treatment is common and does not necessarily indicate treatment failure
Treatment is with the standard multidrug anti-tuberculosis regimen, with surgery reserved for selected complications rather than routine care
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium tuberculosis reaches lymph nodes via lymphatic or haematogenous spread, often from a primary pulmonary focus. Within the node, a cell-mediated immune response forms granulomas with epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells and central caseous necrosis. Progressive necrosis can liquefy to form a cold abscess that may track to the skin and produce a chronically discharging sinus. The relatively contained immune response accounts for the frequent absence of systemic symptoms, while immune reconstitution or the intense host response during therapy can transiently worsen node size (paradoxical reaction).
additionalInvestigations: Fine-needle aspiration cytology for granulomas and caseation
Molecular testing (cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification) and culture of aspirate or tissue
Excisional node biopsy with histopathology when cytology is inconclusive
Chest imaging to assess for concurrent pulmonary or mediastinal disease
HIV testing given the association with extrapulmonary tuberculosis
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging or systemically unwell patient suggesting alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma
Airway or vascular compression from massive mediastinal or cervical nodes
Rifampicin resistance on molecular testing requiring a drug-resistant pathway
reference.prognosis: With the standard multidrug regimen the outlook is excellent, though nodes may enlarge paradoxically during treatment and residual firm nodes or scarring can persist; relapse is uncommon with adherence, and drug resistance worsens outcomes.
pitfalls: Interpreting paradoxical node enlargement during treatment as failure and inappropriately changing therapy
Incising and draining a cold abscess routinely, which risks chronic sinus formation
Missing lymphoma or metastatic carcinoma by not biopsying when cytology is atypical
Overlooking drug-susceptibility testing and HIV status
